content: The Catalogue of Mutations in Mycobacterium tuberculosis Complex and Their Association with Drug Resistance, Second Edition is a comprehensive reference document published by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2023. It provides a detailed and standardized list of genetic mutations in the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC) and their associations with phenotypic drug resistance. This catalogue is intended to serve as a critical resource for interpreting resistance to both first-line and second-line tuberculosis (TB) drugs. The second edition of the catalogue builds upon the first edition, published in 2021, by incorporating new data from a significantly expanded database of whole-genome sequencing (WGS) and phenotypic drug-susceptibility testing (pDST) results. This updated version includes data from approximately 52,000 MTBC isolates collected globally, compared to the 38,000 isolates analyzed in the first edition. The primary goal of this revision was to enhance the detection of genomic variants associated with resistance to both legacy and newly introduced or repurposed TB therapeutics, while also improving the geographical representation of the data. The molecular basis of rifampicin (RIF) resistance in MTBC isolates is predominantly due to mutations in the rifampicin resistance-determining region (RRDR) of the rpoB gene, an 81-base-pair fragment. This knowledge has been instrumental in the development of molecular diagnostic tools targeting RRDR, which have significantly improved the rapid detection of RIF resistance. WHO recommends routine testing of all TB patients for resistance to RIF and isoniazid (INH), with additional testing for fluoroquinolone (FQ) resistance in cases of RIFor INH-resistant TB. Molecular tools for detecting mutations associated with resistance to these drugs are commercially available and endorsed by WHO. The introduction of new TB drugs and the repurposing of existing antimicrobial agents have expanded treatment options for TB. However, the emergence of resistance to these new and repurposed drugs has raised concerns about the lack of rapid diagnostic tools for detecting such resistance. To address this, WHO has recently recommended targeted next-generation sequencing (NGS) assays for culture-free diagnosis of drug-resistant TB. These assays provide direct sequencing from sputum samples and offer broader genomic coverage of resistance-associated regions compared to traditional genotypic drug-susceptibility testing (gDST) assays. However, their sensitivity for predicting resistance to certain drugs remains limited due to incomplete understanding of the molecular mechanisms of resistance. The second edition of the catalogue aims to address these challenges by providing a standardized reference for interpreting resistance to all first-line drugs (RIF, INH, ethambutol [EMB], and pyrazinamide [PZA]) and second-line drugs, including those in Group A (levofloxacin [LFX], moxifloxacin [MFX], bedaquiline [BDQ], and linezolid [LZD]), Group B (clofazimine [CFZ]), and Group C (delamanid [DLM], amikacin [AMK], streptomycin [STM], ethionamide [ETO], and prothionamide [PTO]). While kanamycin (KAN) and capreomycin (CAP) are no longer recommended for use, the catalogue provides data on resistance to these drugs for historical and research purposes. The development of this document was led by a team of experts, including Nazir Ahmed Ismail, Carl-Michael Nathanson, and Alexei Korobitsyn, with support from Matteo Zignol and under the overall direction of Tereza Kasaeva, Director of the WHO Global TB Programme. The data curation, analysis, and algorithm development were conducted by a multidisciplinary team of researchers from institutions worldwide, including FIND (Geneva, Switzerland), the University of California San Diego (USA), the University of Cambridge (UK), and others. The catalogue is based on a systematic analysis of a large WHO database of WGS and pDST data from clinical MTBC isolates collected globally. It includes confidence-graded genetic markers of phenotypic resistance, distinguishing variants statistically associated with resistance from those not associated or lacking sufficient data for meaningful association. This approach reduces uncertainty regarding the number, identity, and clinical interpretation of genomic resistance-determining regions for TB drugs. WHO emphasizes that the use of this catalogue should not imply endorsement of any specific organization, product, or service. The document is distributed under a Creative Commons license, allowing non-commercial use, adaptation, and redistribution with appropriate citation. Any adaptations must be licensed under the same or equivalent terms, and translations must include a disclaimer indicating that WHO is not responsible for the content or accuracy of the translation. The second edition of the catalogue represents a significant step forward in the global effort to combat TB by providing a robust and standardized tool for the interpretation of drug resistance. It is expected to play a central role in improving TB diagnostics, guiding treatment decisions, and ultimately reducing the burden of drug-resistant TB worldwide.
